blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 6.1.2 (there is no 6.1.1 in the book); the portal numbers it 6.1.1 to keep the order.

items: A sequence which consists of a finite number of terms is called a finite sequence. For example, \(2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23\) is a finite sequence of 8 terms.

A sequence which consists of an infinite number of terms is called an infinite sequence. For example, \(3, 10, 17, 24, \ldots\) is an infinite sequence, or more generally \(3, 10, 17, 24, \ldots, 7n-4, \ldots\), to show how each term was generated.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to tell them apart: a finite sequence stops; its last term is written. An infinite sequence never stops; the three dots "\(\ldots\)" at the end mean "and so on for ever".
Where does \(7n - 4\) come from? Each term of \(3, 10, 17, 24, \ldots\) is 7 more than the one before, so the rule has \(7n\); and \(7(1) - 4 = 3\) fixes the constant. Check: \(7(2) - 4 = 10\), \(7(3) - 4 = 17\), \(7(4) - 4 = 24\).
Writing the general term inside the list, "\(\ldots, 7n-4, \ldots\)", tells the reader exactly how every term is made.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: If a sequence is given, then we can find its \(n\)th term, and if the \(n\)th term of a sequence is given, then we can find the terms of the sequence.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem: Find the first four terms of the sequences whose \(n\)th terms are given. (i) \(a_{n} = 3n + 1\) (ii) \(a_{n} = 3n^{2} - 3\)
steps:
Given: (i) \(a_{n} = 3n + 1\); (ii) \(a_{n} = 3n^{2} - 3\).
To find: the first four terms \(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}\) of each sequence.
Method: the \(n\)th term is a rule in \(n\), so we substitute \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\) one by one.

Step 1: (i) Put \(n = 1\) in \(a_{n} = 3n + 1\)
\[a_{1} = 3(1) + 1 = 4\]
Why: \(a_{1}\) is the term in position 1, so \(n\) is replaced by 1.

Step 2: (i) Put \(n = 2, 3, 4\)
\[a_{2} = 3(2) + 1 = 7\]
\[a_{3} = 3(3) + 1 = 10\]
\[a_{4} = 3(4) + 1 = 13\]
Why: the same rule gives every term; only the position changes.
The first four terms are \(4, 7, 10, 13\).

Step 3: (ii) Put \(n = 1\) in \(a_{n} = 3n^{2} - 3\)
\[a_{1} = 3(1)^{2} - 3 = 0\]
Why: square \(n\) first, then multiply by 3, then subtract 3 (order of operations).

Check:
(i) the terms go up by 3 each time (\(4, 7, 10, 13\)), as expected from \(3n\).
(ii) \(a_{n} = 3(n^{2} - 1)\): for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\) we get \(3 \times 0, 3 \times 3, 3 \times 8, 3 \times 15\), that is \(0, 9, 24, 45\).

blocks.text: Sequences of numbers which follow specific patterns are called progressions. Depending on the pattern, progressions are classified as follows.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick preview of the three types (each has its own section later in this unit):
Arithmetic: a fixed number is added each time, e.g. \(5, 11, 17, 23, \ldots\) (add 6).
Geometric: each term is multiplied by a fixed number, e.g. \(6, 12, 24, 48, \ldots\) (multiply by 2).
Harmonic: the reciprocals of the terms form an arithmetic progression, e.g. \(1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \ldots\) because \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) is arithmetic.
Sequence (i) of Example 1 is arithmetic; sequence (ii) (\(0, 9, 24, 45\)) is none of these, since neither its differences \(9, 15, 21\) nor its ratios are constant.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A finite sequence has a last term; an infinite sequence goes on without end (shown by "\(\ldots\)").
2. Given the terms we can find the \(n\)th term; given the \(n\)th term we can find any term.
3. To find a term from \(a_{n}\), substitute its position for \(n\).
4. Progressions are sequences with specific patterns: arithmetic, geometric and harmonic.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Squaring the product instead of \(n\): \(3(4)^{2} = 48\), not \((12)^{2} = 144\).
2. Starting with \(n = 0\): the first term is \(a_{1}\), so substitution starts at \(n = 1\).
3. Calling a long list "infinite": a list is infinite only if it never ends; \(2, 5, \ldots, 23\) with a last term is finite.
